B
This is the fundamental geometric interpretation of a definite integral. Integration is the process of summing up an infinite number of infinitesimally small areas (like rectangles) under a curve to find the exact total area within a specific interval.

C
The derivative of a function at a point gives the instantaneous rate of change, which geometrically is the slope (or steepness) of the tangent line to the curve at that exact point.

B
The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus states that differentiation and integration are inverse operations; differentiating an integral of a function returns the original function, and integrating the derivative of a function returns the original function (plus a constant).

B
The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus states that the area under a continuous function f(x) from a to b is the definite integral, which can be evaluated by finding an antiderivative F(x) and calculating F(b) - F(a).

C
This is a direct application of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, which states that the derivative of an area accumulation function F(b) is the value of the original function, f(b), at that upper limit. The slope is the derivative.
